newsitem.title: USA: Supply glut softens Nigerian impact on oil market.
newsitem.headline: Supply glut softens Nigerian impact on oil market.

text.p: A glut of crude oil supplies worldwide has softened the market impact of a forced cutback in Nigerian production, but prices could come under pressure if the crisis is prolonged, traders said on Thursday.

Communal unrest in Nigeria, a key supplier to refiners in the United States, Europe and Asia, has cut output by 10 percent or about 210,000 barrels per day (bpd) since Saturday, and now threatens to disrupt exports.
U.S. buyers so far have shrugged off a warning by top producer Royal Dutch/Shell that it may be forced to cancel or delay exports early next month unless its production is restored.
The last batch of 127 Nigerian hostages working for Shell was freed by local tribesmen on Thursday, portending a possible resolution to the crisis.
The Anglo-Dutch oil giant, which pumps about half of the country's daily flows of 2.15 million barrels, is so far the only equity producer that has been affected by the unrest.

"The general attitude is one of no concern whatsoever," a U.S.-based trader said. "The wet market is soft enough to absorb the temporary loss of 200,000 bpd. If it gets extended to a longer period, maybe it would have an effect."
Another trader on the Gulf Coast echoed that sentiment. "Until something actually happens, with how weak the market is right now, we're not concerned."

A trader at one of the U.S. equity producers in Nigeria was equally dismissive. "Typically problems get resolved in Nigeria. Few problems at the end of the day end up affecting oil production," he said.
Tepid European and Asian demand has expanded spot availabilities of Nigerian crude in recent weeks, and several cargoes with end-April delivery are still looking for homes.
One trader estimated that one million to 1.5 million barrels of Nigerian crude is still available for the end of April and early May.
Nigerian spot prices so far have sustained a feeble tone, reflecting the market's fundamental weakness, traders said.

Forcados, one of two Nigerian grades that have been cut as a result of the crisis, was on offer at a discount of 85 cents to May West Texas Intermediate/Midland for end-April arrival in the U.S., traders said.
Bonny Light, the other affected grade, was pegged at an equivalent of dated Brent plus 25 cents on an fob basis.
Not everyone was prepared to overlook the crisis.

"People are not concerned about this because there's so much crude around...but I think people are getting too complacent," said Mohammed Abduljabbar, senior economist with the Petroleum Finance Co in Washington, D.C.

Abduljabbar pointed to the recent rise in U.S. refinery runs and the upcoming gasoline season as cause for concern. "Two hundred thousand barrels of Nigerian crude is no joke. I think it will affect the market."
The May NYMEX contract was trading around $20.70 a barrel Thursday afternoon, up six cents from Wednesday's settlement.
The leading U.S. buyers of Nigerian crude include Diamond Shamrock, Sun Oil Co, Clark, Mobil, Tosco, Koch Oil, Amerada Hess and Amoco.
